newsitem.title: UK: Zaire mining deal gets a cautious welcome.
newsitem.headline: Zaire mining deal gets a cautious welcome.

text.p: A $1 billion deal between Zaire rebels and a big Western mining company on Tuesday underscored the African country's vast potential as a supplier of minerals to the global economy.

But traders and analysts added that they doubted if the deal, or what seemed to be a likely rebel victory in the civil war, would have much short-term impact on supply or prices of copper, cobalt and zinc.
"I don't see any immediate change in the next few months for mining projects to come to fruition," said Emin Eyi, who is on the African mining desk at HSBC James Capel.
"Zaire would do well to emulate neighbour Zambia, which has been attracting fresh investment after implementing reforms and going forward with privatisation plans," he added.

On Wednesday America Mineral Fields Inc signed an agreement worth $1 billion with Zaire's rebels to buy the Kolwezi copper/cobalt tailings project and build a 200,000 tonnes a year zinc plant at Kipushi.
The agreement was signed by AMF's Jean-Raymonde Boulle and by financial commissioner Mwana Nanga Mawampanga for the Laurent Kabila's rebel alliance.

The deal involves deposits and mines under the control of Zaire's state-owned Gecamines which will be exploited and modernised by America Mineral Fields as a joint venture, with the U.S. company controlling 51 percent and Kabila's alliance holding a minority blocking share of 49 percent.
"This is a start of goodwill and I am very encouraged by it...but for me it's still a little early," Eyi said.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has vowed to stamp out the corruption that critics allege marked President Mobutu Sese Sese's 32 years of rule.
The rebels now control around 50 percent of Zaire and look to be fully in charge in mineral-rich Shaba province and the diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi.
Other Canadian firms like AMF, including Tenke Mining Corp, and South African mining groups, are showing renewed interest in the mineral wealth of Zaire .
"Zaire is a treasure trove of minerals...it's too important for the mining companies to ignore," said Eyi.
But another metals analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity, echoed his note of caution on the pace of events in Zaire.

"It's all very well for a rebel government-in-waiting to sign an agreement with an overseas mining company, but the reality is that we don't yet know who the government will be or what the government is going to look like," he said.
A cobalt trader was blunt in voicing his scepticism when he said that "Zaire remains a whole can of worms still...there is still no sign of complete stability".
Some traders reckoned it might be a decade before the full impact of new foreign investment in Zaire's mining industries, starved of funds under Mobutu, is felt.

In the early 1980s cobalt production was around 15,000 tonnes, versus current levels around 5,000 - although this is still about one-fifth of global production. Output of copper has slumped from around 500,000 tonnes to only about 40,000.
Traders said state-owned Gecamines continues to hold the key to short-term supply and any impact on prices.
Opinions vary on Gecamines present state of play.

Several market sources suggest that Gecamines is still producing and exporting cobalt. On Monday the chief executive officer of Belgium's Union Miniere, Karel Vinck, said supplies from Zaire were still flowing. Vinck said that rail transport routes through South Africa were still running.
Some trade sources say they are sceptical and that Gecamines were not selling on the spot or forward market. "Even if they are producing, no material is flowing from the region," one said.
Traders agreed in seeing the rebels as anxious to boost hard currency exports, although they thought that new contracts with consumers would have to be drawn up.
At the height of the advance by rebel forces and the subsequent fall of the mining capital, Lubumbashi, high grade cobalt traded above $25 a pound. It has eased slightly.
